title: Pippi Longstocking
author: Astrid Lindgren
short_summary: A nine-year-old girl moves into a tumbledown house called Villa Villekulla with a monkey, a horse and a suitcase full of gold coins, and no grown-up at all. Her neighbours Tommy and Annika have never seen anything like her: she sleeps with her feet on the pillow, plays tag with the police on the roof, lasts one morning at school, beats the strongest man in the world at the circus, and makes two burglars dance until their legs give out.
extended_summary:
Pippi Longstocking arrives at Villa Villekulla by herself, carrying a monkey called Mr. Nilsson and leading a horse that she lifts onto the veranda with her own arms. Her mother died when she was a baby and her father, a sea captain, was blown overboard in a storm; Pippi is quite certain he was washed ashore on an island and made king there, and that he will come for her one day. In the meantime she lives alone, pays for everything out of a suitcase of gold coins, and does exactly as she likes. Next door live Tommy and Annika, who are polite, punctual and about to have the best year of their lives.

What follows is not one story but a run of collisions between Pippi and the ordinary world. She declares herself a Thing-Finder and spends a morning picking up whatever the town has dropped. Two policemen come to take her to a children's home and leave by way of the roof, set down outside the gate with a cookie each. She goes to school for a single morning, argues with the teacher about arithmetic, draws a horse on the floor because the paper is too small, and rides home. She bakes five hundred cookies rolled out on the kitchen floor and cleans the floor afterwards with scrubbing brushes tied to her feet.

The strength is real, and Lindgren keeps proving it. At the circus Pippi beats the strongest man in the world in front of the whole town. When two burglars break in for the suitcase, she lifts them up onto the wardrobe, dances them round the room until they beg to stop, and then pays them a gold coin each for their trouble. She climbs into a burning house on a plank and carries two small boys out. At her own birthday party she gives the presents away to her guests. The book never argues that a child should live without grown-ups — it simply lets one do it, for as long as the story lasts.

questions.prompt: Pippi owns a horse. Where does she keep it?

options: On the veranda of her own house
In a stable behind the garden
In the field by the schoolhouse
In the kitchen next to the stove

questions.explanation: She lifts it up there herself, and takes it down again when she wants to ride. The horse on the veranda is the first sign the book gives you that Pippi's strength is not a joke or an exaggeration — it is simply a fact, and everybody in the town has to get used to it.

questions.prompt: Two policemen arrive to take Pippi away to a children's home. How does she deal with them?

options: She plays tag with them all over the roof
She hides in the attic until they leave
She lets her horse chase them down the road
She shows them a letter from her father

questions.explanation: She is delighted — she thinks they have come to play. When the game is over she picks them both up, carries them out through the gate, sets them down and gives them a cookie each. Nobody is hurt and nobody is rude, which is exactly what makes it impossible to argue with her.

questions.prompt: Pippi sleeps the wrong way round in her bed, with her head under the blanket and her feet up on the ___.
questions.explanation: There is nobody to tell her that beds have a top and a bottom, so she has worked out her own arrangement and finds it very comfortable. Lindgren fills the book with small details like this one, where the rule Pippi is breaking turns out to be a rule nobody could explain anyway.

questions.prompt: Pippi goes to school for one morning. What happens there?

options: She argues about arithmetic and draws a horse on the floor
She is the best pupil in the class for one whole day
She teaches the other children how to walk on their hands
She falls asleep at her own desk and is sent home early

questions.explanation: She only came because Tommy and Annika told her about the holidays. The horse gets drawn on the floor because the paper is too small for it, and she leaves before lunch. The teacher, to her great credit, never once loses her temper.

questions.prompt: Put these events from Pippi's year at Villa Villekulla in the order they happen.

items: Pippi moves in and meets Tommy and Annika
She spends a morning hunting for lost things
Two policemen try to take her to a children's home
She goes to school for one single morning
She beats the strongest man in the world at the circus
Two burglars break in and are made to dance
She gives away all the presents at her own birthday party

questions.explanation: The book is built as a series of separate mornings and afternoons rather than one long plot, which is why it can be read a chapter at a time. Notice that the order still matters: the town has to meet Pippi before it can try to correct her, and it has to fail at correcting her before it can start enjoying her.

questions.prompt: Match each part of Pippi's household to what it actually is.

right: A small monkey who wears a straw hat
The polite children who live next door
Her father, lost overboard in a storm
Full of gold coins, and pays for everything

questions.explanation: Put together, these four answer the question the grown-ups keep asking: how can a child live alone? She has money, company, and a father she expects back. Lindgren is careful to give Pippi everything except supervision.

questions.prompt: Tommy and Annika live one way and Pippi lives another. Sort each item into the right household.

content.groupA: Life next door at Tommy and Annika's

options.label: Dinner at the table at the same time each day
Bed when a grown-up says it is bedtime
Off to school every single morning
Sleeping with your feet up on the pillow
Five hundred cookies rolled out on the floor
Scrubbing the floor with brushes on your feet

questions.explanation: The left-hand column is not written as a bad life, and that is the point — Tommy and Annika are happy, and they are the ones who get to visit. Lindgren lets the reader have both: the ordinary house to come home to, and the extraordinary one next door.

questions.prompt: Pippi goes to the circus. What does she end up doing there?

options: She beats the strongest man in the world
She is thrown out before the show starts
She buys the whole circus with her gold
She rides away on the circus master's horse

questions.explanation: The strongman challenge is offered to the audience and Pippi simply takes it, in front of the entire town. This is the moment the townspeople can no longer pretend she is an ordinary child telling tall stories, and after it nobody tries to send her to a children's home again.

questions.prompt: Two burglars break into Villa Villekulla to steal Pippi's suitcase of gold. What does she do to them?

options: She makes them dance, then pays them for it
She locks them in the wardrobe until morning
She gives them the suitcase and waves goodbye
She calls the two policemen back to the house

questions.explanation: First she lifts them onto the top of the wardrobe, then she dances them round the room until they are exhausted, and then — because they danced with her — she gives them a gold coin each and some food. She is never cruel and never frightened, and the burglars leave more confused than punished.

questions.prompt: Pippi has no job and no parents, but she never runs out of money, because she keeps a whole suitcase full of gold ___.
questions.explanation: Her father gave it to her, and she treats it as something to spend on other people: cookies for policemen, presents for guests, a gold piece for burglars who danced nicely. Notice that the money never makes her want anything for herself.

questions.prompt: Imagine a new grown-up moves to the town and tells Pippi that children cannot possibly live alone. Based on how she behaves in the book, what would most likely happen?

options: She would treat it as a game and win it cheerfully
She would shout at the grown-up and slam the door
She would agree and move in with Tommy and Annika
She would hide in the house until the grown-up left

questions.explanation: Pippi never wins an argument by arguing. The policemen, the teacher, the ladies at the coffee party and the burglars are all handled the same way — she is friendly, she is unbudgeable, and the grown-up ends up outside holding a cookie and wondering what happened.

questions.prompt: Tommy and Annika have parents, rules and bedtimes. Pippi has none of these, and the book makes her life look wonderful. Do you think Pippi is really better off with no grown-ups at all? Use things that actually happen in the book to explain your answer.
questions.explanation: Both answers can score full marks, and the evidence runs both ways. For 'better off': nobody stops her, she is never lonely for long, and she can handle burglars, policemen and a burning house by herself. Against: she is the only child in the book with no one waiting up for her, she invites Tommy and Annika to everything, and she is still watching the sea for a father who has not come back. Accept any clear position that points at something in the book.

questions.prompt: Pippi calls herself a Thing-Finder: she walks about the town looking for things other people have lost or thrown away, and she is delighted by whatever she picks up. Invent one thing-finding morning for her. Where does she look, what does she find, and what does she decide to do with it?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. What makes an invention feel like Pippi is the second half: she never finds treasure, she finds a rusty tin can or an old spool and then explains, quite seriously, what it is really for. A find that is genuinely valuable has missed the joke.
